newsitem.title: DUBAI: Most on crashed Saudi airliner Indians, Nepalese. [CORRECTED 19:50 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Most on crashed Saudi airliner Indians, Nepalese. [CORRECTED 19:50 GMT]

text.p: Most of the passengers aboard a Saudi jumbo jet involved in a mid-air collision over India on Tuesday were from India and Nepal, Saudi-owned Middle East Broadcasting Corp (MBC) television said.
Nearly 350 people were feared dead when the Saudi Boeing 747 and a Kazakhstan airliner collided west of New Delhi, the Press Trust of India reported.
The London-based satellite channel, quoting a Saudi Arabian Airlines Corp official in New Delhi, said Europeans were also among the passenger list. It did not specify their nationalities.
There was only one Saudi passenger on board the flight from New Delhi to Dhahran in eastern Saudi Arabia, MBC said.
The 312 passengers included eight children, it said. The crew comprised 11 Saudis and eight others from India, the Philippines and Morocco.
Saudi Arabian Airlines is the largest airline in the Middle East. It flies 12.5 million passengers a year.

The airline's last major disaster was in August 1980 (corrects year from 1990) when a Lockheed TriStar aircraft caught fire at Riyadh airport shortly before takeoff. All 301 people aboard were killed.
The state carrier has suffered operating losses for more than a decade mainly due to heavy government subsidies particularly on fares on domestic routes, on which it has a monopoly.
Founded 51 years ago, the airline changed its name from Saudia in July and adopted a new livery for its fleet of 109 aircraft.

The airline is a leading candidate for privatisation when Saudi Arabia begins selling off state assets. It is spending $6 billion on 61 new Boeing and McDonnell Douglas airliners, the first of which are due to enter service next year.
Industry executives say up to 70 percent of its operations are domestic and 30 percent international. But almost 75 percent of its income is generated on international routes.
